The spread of new crops and farming methods across the Islamic world from the 8th century to about the 12th, a name given by the historian Andrew Watson in the 1970s. Crops long grown in India and Southeast Asia moved west to the Middle East, North Africa, al-Andalus and Sicily.

Among them were sugar cane, rice, sour oranges and lemons, cotton, aubergines, spinach, sorghum, hard wheat and bananas. Many of these grow in summer, when Mediterranean lands are dry, so they spread with irrigation: the qanat, water wheels and new rotations that let fields bear crops all year. Farming manuals were written in Arabic, and Spanish still shows the debt in words such as arroz (rice), azúcar (sugar) and naranja (orange).

The vast Abbasid realm helped: one rule stretched from Spain to Central Asia, and travellers, traders and officials carried seeds along with goods. Later historians argue over how new or revolutionary it was, since some crops were known earlier in Roman and Persian lands. Sugar and cotton went on to shape later history, through refined sugar and the Columbian exchange.
